content:
This section is bibliography and index, not argument. File pages 490 through 495 (printed pages 469 through 474) are the tail of the References list, running alphabetically from Marr and Vaina through Zwicky. File pages 496 through 499 (printed pages 475 through 478) are the opening of the Index, covering entries from Abramovitch through External argument. No prose exposition, examples, or reasoning appear here, so there are no central claims to report from these pages themselves.

What the section does provide is a map of the book's concerns. The reference list shows Pinker drawing on learnability theory (Baker, Wexler and Culicover, Osherson, Stob and Weinstein), lexical semantics and argument structure (Rappaport and Levin, Talmy, Dowty, Vendler), developmental psycholinguistics (Bowerman, Brown, Braine), and connectionist modeling (McClelland and Kawamoto; Pinker and Prince 1988, listed at file page 492). The index confirms the book's architecture: argument structure representations and linking rules (file page 496), lexical rules for causative, conative, dative, locative and passive alternations (file pages 496, 498), and Baker's paradox with four candidate solutions, including strict lexical conservatism and syntactic criteria for rule application (file page 497).

The index entries are the most substantive material available. They distinguish broad-range from narrow-range lexical rules and note that only narrow-range rules are existence-predicting rather than merely property-predicting (file page 499), which is exactly the permitted-scope versus memorization distinction the task asks about. Entries also record semantic constraints on children's causatives, datives, locatives and passives (file page 498), children's conservatism and ambivalence about their own errors (file page 498), conflation classes as thematic cores of argument structures (file pages 496, 498), and a cross-linguistic inventory of components of verbal meaning (file page 499). Topics such as perception, memory, time, goals, analogy, creativity, emotions, and social cognition are not indexed in this span; causation appears only as grammatical causative constructions, not as a general theory.

Engineering relevance is therefore indirect. The index suggests a design vocabulary: represent events with typed argument structures, license productive rules by explicit semantic and syntactic criteria rather than by stored exceptions, and separate rules that predict which forms may exist from rules that merely predict properties of known forms. That is a plausible skeleton for a compositional, inspectable symbol system. Nothing in these pages demonstrates that such a system suffices for grounded perception, temporal memory, planning, or general intelligence, and nothing here addresses neural versus non-neural implementation; the restriction to an inspectable non-neural machine is our engineering choice, not a claim attributable to Steven Pinker on this evidence.

Uncertainty: page labels are visible in the running heads (References 469–474; Index 475–478). Some entries contain typographic artifacts from scanning, such as split words and ligature substitutions ("difﬁ culty", "learn è d", "A ﬁ liation"), and one page number in the Pustejovsky 1988 entry appears garbled ("347 – 268"). Index locators point to pages outside this excerpt and were not verified.
